items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the general business law, in relation to publicly accessible collection bins
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S5893

TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the general business law, in relation
to publicly accessible collection bins

PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:  To eliminate collection bins on
public property and to ensure that collection bins on private property
are responsibly maintained and operated.

SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

Section 1. Amends Section 399-bbb of the general business law, This
new section changes the term "collection container bin" to "publicly
accessible collection bin." Additionally, the section prohibits the
public placement of collection bins, and allows local municipalities
to immediately remove and dispose of the bins. This section also
requires, the disclosure of the email address and website, if
applicable, of the person or organization operating the bin on the bin
itself, in addition to the phone number and address, as well as a
statement that nothing should be left outside of the bin. If an agent
represents an owner of a collection bin, including a for-profit entity
on behalf of, or in conjunction with a not-for-profit organization,
that must also be disclosed.

If a bin is operated by a not-for-profit organization, a statement
must be displayed describing the charitable causes that will benefit
from donations. Additionally, collection bins operated by corporate
fundraisers or entities, for the benefit of either another for-profit
or nonprofit entity, must abide by all the disclosures and labeling
requirements in this section of the law, and any additional guidelines
and labeling requirements under state or local law as applicable. The
bins must also display any permits or licenses that are required by
local law, and if required by state or local law, the bins must
display a statement that has contact information for the department of
law for the public to obtain more information.

For publicly accessible collection bins that are placed on private
property with the consent of the owner of the property, consent may be
revoked at any time, provided written notice of the rescission is
given to the bin owner at least ten days prior to the bin's removal.
Written notice of such rescission is deemed given when deposited in a
mailbox properly addressed and adequate postage prepaid. Such written
notice shall be effective regardless of the form of the written notice
if it indicates the intention of the owner or lessee of the property
to rescind the consent previously given by the property owner or
lessee's authorized agent. The property owner or lessee may remove and
dispose of such bin after ten days of providing notice, and any costs
associated with such removal or disposal shall be recoverable from the
owner of the publicly- accessible collection bin.

This section also provides maintenance requirements for bin owners:

-bins must be serviced and emptied as needed, or within three days of
a maintenance request by the property owner, including requests for
removal of debris and bulk items


-the owners must remove graffiti or repair damaged bins within 72
hours of requests or otherwise becoming aware of the vandalism

-the owners must secure collection bins with a tamper resistant lock

-the owners must maintain the aesthetic presentation of such bin,
including fresh paint and readable signage.

This section also provides that property owners are not subject to
civil liability from a collection bin operator for the removal of an
unauthorized bin, or where removal is necessary to comply with state
or local zoning ordinances, as applicable, without giving prior notice
to the bin owner. However, the property owner must inform the bin
operator to where the bin was moved, or any other disposition of the
bin. Additionally, any costs associated with such removal or disposal
shall be recoverable from the owner of the publicly accessible
collection bin.

Civil penalties shall be retained by the municipality or county in
which such bin was placed. Additionally, any bin in violation of the
provisions related to the display of information or unpermitted
placement shall subject the owner of such bin to a civil penalty of
$250 for the first offense, and $500 fine for each subsequent offense
within an 18 month period.

Additionally, any bin in violation of the maintenance provisions shall
subject the owner of such bin to a civil penalty of $50 for the first
offense, and $100 for each subsequent offense within an 18 month
period.

Section 2. Provides the effective date.

JUSTIFICATION:  Clothing collection bins have proliferated throughout
New York City and State to such an extent that there are often two or
three bins within a few blocks of another. These bins are often not
maintained by their operators, and have served as trash receptacles
for the public. While collection bins have long been considered a
positive way to donate used clothing to those in need, collection bins
are sometimes operated by irresponsible companies masquerading as
charities. Legislation to ban collection bins on public property is
necessary to curb this scourge on New York's neighborhoods.

This legislation adds maintenance requirements for the collection
bins, and requires that disclosures be made by owners of the bins.
The disclosures include whether or not a bin is operated by a
non-profit organization or a for-profit business, or whether a bin is
operated by a for-profit business in conjunction with a non-profit
organization, a practice referred to as "rent-a-charity."

In December, New York City signed legislation that does not take
effect until March 2015. This legislation would harmonize with and
strengthen the forthcoming New York City law.

This legislation has been drafted with assistance from Secondary
Materials And Recycled Textiles (SMART), an association that
represents the wiping materials, used clothing, and fiber industries,


with the goal of weeding out bad actors while not negatively impacting
the responsible operators who are from these trades.

This legislation would also add maintenance requirements for
collection bins for towns and municipalities throughout New York
State, as neighborhoods in other parts of New York, such as Nassau and
Suffolk Counties, have encountered similar problems with collection
bins. The legislation would allow for the immediate removal of the
bins by the towns if the bins are placed on public property and also
provides guidance for private property owners who permit bins on their
property.

PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:  None.

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:  None.

EFFECTIVE DATE:  This act shall take effect on the one hundred
eightieth day after it shall have become a law and shall apply to all
publicly accessible collection bins in place on the effective date of
this act and all publicly accessible collection bins placed subsequent
to the effective date of this act.
